claims.text: Explicitly incorporating defect-induced scattering into an integrated DFT and machine-learning framework will improve conductivity predictions for bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed framework will match experimental conductivity within ±10% over 0–200 K.
The proposed framework will match experimental conductivity within ±10% over 300–1200 K.
Including 1 wt.% oxygen impurities and intrinsic defects will overcome limitations associated with perfect-crystal conductivity models.
Sampling oxygen defects, vacancies, and local lattice distortions will provide suitable training data for a machine-learning conductivity model.
Electron scattering by defects dominates conductivity behavior in HfNbTaTiZr over 0–200 K.
Phonon-related conduction and defect–phonon interactions dominate conductivity behavior over 300–1200 K.
Isolated oxygen defects, vacancy clusters, and associated local lattice distortions mediate scattering processes in bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
These defect structures affect electron mean free paths.
These defect structures affect phonon lifetimes.
Defects alter the electronic band structure of HfNbTaTiZr.
Defects modify the phonon dispersion of HfNbTaTiZr.
Accounting for electron–defect and phonon scattering will produce more realistic temperature-dependent conductivity predictions than perfect-crystal analytical models.
At approximately 1050 K, the conductivity is expected to be around 4.5×10^5 S/m.
The model will capture pronounced defect-driven suppression of conductivity over 0–200 K.
Conventional perfect-crystal analytical methods deviate significantly from experiment because they neglect realistic scattering mechanisms.
The framework is applicable to as-synthesized bulk HfNbTaTiZr, with and without 1 wt.% oxygen, over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Temperatures outside the stated ranges may involve different dominant scattering processes and require additional calibration.
